summary: The entry is anchored by a precisely cited question from the published literature: Kulaichev (1984) asked whether his rigid Śrī Yantra is unique, and Chiodo (C. R. Math. 2021) says that question is still open. A certified uniqueness theorem for it is plausibly worth a research note, for specialists in certified real-algebraic computation, in formal verification of geometric constraint systems and in the mathematical history of the Śrī Yantra. The literature account is careful and checkable. The quotations checked against Chiodo match the text. The prior numerical work (Rao, Pustynski) and the golden-ratio drawings (Bolton and Macleod, Fonseca) are placed accurately, and sources that were not read are disclosed precisely. The second theorem added in Version 2 has a much weaker claim to independent interest. Its fourth condition comes from the submitter's own unreviewed papers, and no outside source asks for it. The account itself says no theorem singles it out among several alternatives. What would make it interesting, that the figure has the traditional counts, is certified outside Lean and is not part of the compared statements.

findings.evidence: Challenge header, 'Second theorem' and 'The golden product is one choice among several'; Yantra.GoldenProduct; golden_unique, golden_slope
findings.message: The research interest of the new theorem pair (golden_unique, golden_slope) is not established independently of the Kulaichev theorems. The golden slope product uv = 2/φ³ was introduced in the submitter's own unreviewed work, and no published source asks for it. The account itself states that no theorem singles it out among the other fourth conditions listed in #103, Table 3. The property that would give it outside interest, that the unique figure has the traditional 43 triangles and 24 sandhis, is not in the Lean statements. As formalised, the new theorem is a uniqueness result for one chosen condition in a family the account calls arbitrary. The entry is acceptable as a companion to the answer to Kulaichev's question, and the account discloses all of this honestly. To stand on its own, the new theorem needs either an outside reason to single out this condition or the traditional counts stated and proved in Lean.

internal_notes.message: Every Chiodo quotation in the account was checked word for word: p. 381 (French, uniqueness 'toujours ouverte'), §1.2.4 (English, 'out of reach … not considered here'), and §1.2.2 with n. 15 (Bolton and Macleod and Fonseca golden-ratio constructions fail concurrency in a way not visible to the eye). The bibliographic details are correct: vol. 359, no. 4, pp. 377–397, doi 10.5802/crmath.163. Chiodo's [18, 21, 23, 24] (Pustynski, Santhi et al., Tahta, Tularam) are all listed in the account as read or as not read, so no item Chiodo cites near Kulaichev is missing.

Positive evidence of notability: a published question (IJHS 1984, p. 285) that a C. R. Math. author called open in 2021, answered by certified computation and checked by Lean's kernel. Pustynski's 2014 grid-plot 'proof' is correctly described as non-rigorous, so no priority problem was found. The audience is specialised but identifiable.

Taken alone, the golden-product theorem would be borderline under the notability anchors. A credible audience beyond the Kulaichev question is not shown, and the condition is drawn from the submitter's own unreviewed Zenodo papers (#29, #44, #103). The entry passes as a whole because the account is honest about the choice (Table 3 alternatives, 'no theorem singles the golden product out') and because it makes no historical claim.

The account separates the golden product from the Bolton–Macleod and Fonseca drawings fairly: an exact equation on an exactly concurrent figure, versus approximate drawings. The non-constructibility argument (degree 160 is not a power of 2, so Wantzel applies) is correct as stated, given #103's irreducibility theorem. Bolton and Macleod and Fonseca are closed access and disclosed as not read; their content is relayed via Chiodo (verified) and Kulaichev and Gupta (not independently fetched). This is not a defect.

The record page says a newer version exists, so the citation should name the concept DOI or the latest version. The unblinded record title is promotional ('Overcoming the Seemingly Impossible, Towards Perfection') and uses the submitter's names for the condition and the yantra. That belongs to the metadata step, not this one, but the metadata reviewer should note it.

The INSA/Jain-hosted PDF returned 404, so the quotations on p. 274 and §2.5 were not checked independently. A search snippet agrees with the account's description (polynomial degree bound 12544, a uniqueness argument). This is a tooling limit, not a finding.
Independent search found no Śrī Yantra formalisation in any proof assistant other than the submitter's own Version 1. This agrees with the account.

what_would_reach_higher: Formalise the region counts in Lean (43 triangles and 24 sandhis for the golden-product figure; 45 regions with 4 four-sided and 28 sandhis for Kulaichev's), so that the contrast which motivates Version 2 is part of the compared statements and is not certified only outside Lean.

Give an outside or theorem-level reason to single out uv = 2/φ³ among the Table 3 conditions. For example, prove a characterisation (such as the exact boundary in the space of fourth conditions where the two extra triangles appear) and formalise it, or show that a published source asks for this condition.

Alternatively, generalise golden_unique to a theorem about the whole one-parameter family uv = c (uniqueness over an interval of c, and which c give the traditional counts). That makes the result less dependent on one chosen constant.

Get #103 refereed (for example in a journal of computational geometry or history of mathematics) and cite the refereed version. Cite the Zenodo concept DOI or the latest version, since the record says a newer version exists.

Obtain and read Bolton and Macleod (1977) and Fonseca (1986), for example via interlibrary loan or by writing to the authors. Then confirm first-hand that neither paper imposes a golden-ratio slope product on an exactly concurrent figure.
Re-check the Pustynski quotations against a working copy (the hosted PDF now returns 404) and give a stable URL.
Send the result to someone working on this topic (for example Chiodo) and record any reply as evidence that people outside the project find the golden-product theorem interesting.
